draft.title: Resistance to change
card: Resistance to change is when people or groups oppose or try to block a change. It can be open, such as a protest, or quiet, such as ignoring a new rule.
People may resist to protect tradition, identity, power or security. A group may fear losing customs, a sense of who they are, their influence, or their jobs and safety.
Resistance does not always stop change. It can slow change down, or it can reshape it so the final change looks different from the first plan.
Resistance can come from any group, including those with little power. The same change may be welcomed by some people and resisted by others.
draft.remember: People resist change to protect what matters to them, and this can slow or reshape the change.

a.q: Why might a village elder oppose a plan to replace a traditional ceremony with a modern festival?
opts: To protect tradition and the community's identity
To speed up the change so it ends sooner
To show that the change has already finished
To bring in a new technology as an agent of change
a.why: The elder is acting to protect tradition and identity, two common reasons for resistance. Speeding up the change is the opposite of resisting it.
a.clue: What is the elder trying to keep?

b.q: A council in Ballarat plans to close a small rural bus route. Residents protest, and the council keeps the route but runs it less often. What did the resistance do?
opts: It reshaped the change, as the result differed from the plan
It stopped the change completely, as nothing was altered
It had no effect, as the council still made a change
It sped up the change, as the council acted quickly
b.why: The route was kept but run less often, so the result differed from the first plan. That is reshaping. It did not stop change completely, because the service still changed.
b.clue: Compare the final outcome with the first plan.

a.best: To protect tradition and the community's identity

b.best: It reshaped the change, as the result differed from the plan

problems.detail: Too easy for Year 12. The distractors ('to show that the change has already finished', 'to speed up the change so it ends sooner') are implausible reasons for opposing a change, so a student can pick the right option without knowing the idea.

In Victoria, bus routes in places like Ballarat are planned and contracted by the state transport department, not the local council. A council closing a bus route is unrealistic in Australia. A state transport authority would be more accurate.

a.q: Taxi drivers in Sydney protest when a ride-share app arrives, as they fear they will earn less. What are they mainly trying to protect?
opts: Their jobs and the security of their income
A custom passed down through many generations
Their influence over decisions made by government
Their sense of who they are as a cultural group
a.why: The drivers fear earning less, so they are protecting their jobs and income, which is security. Nothing in the case is about a custom, political influence or cultural identity, so those reasons do not fit.
a.clue: Look at what the drivers fear losing.

b.q: A state transport authority plans to close a small rural bus route near Ballarat. Residents protest, and the route is kept but runs less often. What did the resistance do?
opts: It reshaped the change, as the result differed from the plan
It stopped the change completely, as nothing was altered
It had no effect, as the authority still made a change
It sped up the change, as the authority acted quickly
b.why: The route was kept but run less often, so the result differed from the first plan. That is reshaping. It did not stop change completely, because the service still changed.
b.clue: Compare the final outcome with the first plan.

a.best: Their jobs and the security of their income

b.best: It reshaped the change, as the result differed from the plan
